segments.text: A Topology-Aware Selection and Duty Control Algorithm for Comparative Performance Enhancement of Electric Vehicle Power Converters Abstract- The electrification of automotive applications cannot succeed without EV power conversion systems that have a critical impact on drivetrain efficiency, thermal robustness and energy consumption for traction, regenerative braking and charging modes. While significant literature exists in evaluating isolated DC–DC and bidirectional converter topologies, the majority of the studies are focused on static conditions with fixed values which do not capture the highly fluctuating power requirements in practical EV operation. In this paper, we introduce a novel TADS (Topology-Aware Duty and Selection) algorithm for EV power converters that provides an organized and fair comparison while improving systemlevel performance, without introducing computation-intensive or adaptive control strategies. The presented methodology combines few number of industry oriented converter topologies by employing a rule based topology selection strategy that takes into consideration the power requirement, level ratio and the thermal conditions through duty cycle computation for selected topologies. Unlike traditional comparative analysis, which relies on a single 'best' topology assumption, TADS dynamically chooses the best converter topology with respect to different operating conditions such as acceleration, cruising and regenerative braking and charging regimes. The simulation results using standard EV drive cycles show that the average efficiency improvement of the proposed method compared to fixed topology based converter systems is 2.8%, peak switching losses decrease by 18.6%, and the maximum junction temperature decreases by 14.2%. Furthermore, the whole efficiency of the energy use during full-cycle operations is enhanced by 3.4%. These findings confirm that the proposed topology-aware framework is a viable and sized approach to next-generation EV power electronics, providing performance improvements without sacrificing implementation simplicity. Keywords- Electric vehicles, DC–DC converters, power electronics, topology selection, duty cycle control, efficiency optimization, comparative study. 1. Introduction Electric vehicles (EVs) have become a key solution for sustainable transportation by promising to largely mitigate the vehicles’ greenhouse gas emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. On the core of an EV powertrain stands power electronic conversion system [1][2] that mainly controls bi-directional energy flows between battery pack, traction inverter, and auxiliary subsystems [3][4], along with external charging infrastructure [5]. Transistorized dc–dc and bidirectional converters are important
segments.label: human

segments.text: to maintain voltage regulation, efficient transfer of energy and protection of delicate devices against electrical overstress and thermal excursions [6][7]. The efficiency of these converters can directly affect overall vehicle performance, battery life time, thermal reliability and driving range of the vehicle; therefore power conversion have become a critical design concern in current EV architectures [8]. There have been a lot of works focusing on DC–DC converter topologies for EV in recent years, such as buck [9], boost, buck–boost, interleaved, isolated and bidirectional topologies [10]. Although these studies help understand the converter behavior, but also most of the comparison is done under constant operation [11] what means that there is a single topology and direct duty ratio. The above methods do not account for the intrinsic dynamic behavior of the EV, since rapid modes-switches take place among acceleration, cruising at constant speed in steady-state condition, regenerative braking and recharging ones, each one entailing different power and thus DC voltage levels and thermal loads on the converter fringe system [12]. Furthermore, the few current comparative frameworks usually consider individual performance metrics, such as peak efficiency or voltage gain [13] at best and disregard system-level implications over a driving cycle [14]. Advanced control techniques such as model predictive control and artificial intelligence–based approaches have been investigated to accommodate dynamic operation, but with tradeoffs of high computational burden, additional sensing, and limited industrial applicability for wide installation [16], [18], [35]. As a result, there is still an urgent demand for a practical and scalable platform to facilitate fair comparison and efficient utilization of multiple converter topologies under real EV-operating scenarios. To mitigate these limitations, this work presents three research objectives: (i) lack of a consistent framework for dynamic and fair comparison of various converter topologies, (ii) absence of topology-aware duty cycle calculation as a function of varying operating regions and (iii) limited investigations on system-level efficiency and thermal performance across standardized EV drive cycles. Closing such gaps is important for the further development of next generation EV power electronics, which reconciles improving performance with circuit complexity. In this context, this article introduces a new Topology-Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) methodology for the EV power converters. The method includes a library of commercially representative DC–DC and bidirectional converters topologies and uses rule-based selection based on power requirement, voltage step-ratio, and heat-flow limitation. In contrast to traditional studies which consider a single best-fit topology, the TADS method adaptively determines the adequate converter configuration for each working region, and solves for its respective duty cycle in a topologically
segments.label: human

segments.text: equivalent manner. This allows a fair comparative evaluation while obtaining measurable benefits in terms of efficiency, switching losses and thermal stress in relevant driving conditions. The salient features of the paper are: ●​ A Topology-aware duty And Selection (TAD S) algorithm for dynamic selection and fair comparison of EV DC-DC converter topologies at different operating points. ●​ An easy rule based duty and topology control scheme, which increases both efficiency and thermal performance without resorting to complex adaptive or intelligent controllers. The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 presents literature review of the DC–DC converter topologies and comparison studies for EV. The model of the EV power conversion system and the inc-luded converter topologies are presented in Section 3. The proposed TADS algorithm and its rule-based selection logic are presented in Section 4. The simulation setup and evaluation methodology is described in Section 5. Section 6 presents the comparative performance results at representative EV drive cycles. Last, Section 7 ends the paper and discusses some directions for future work. 2. Literature Review​ Rathore et al. (2022) proposed a dedicated stand-alone multilevel DC–DC converter configuration for fast charging in electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The design of aimed at high power density and small filter size by generating multilevel output voltages using the voltage doubler rectifier units. Soft-switching was obtained due to resonance between leakage inductance of transformer and parasitic capacitances, opening the possibility to improve efficiency at higher power levels. While the topology had good behavior for fast charging, its design was only tuned at a fixed point and not capable of dealing with the number of operating conditions encountered by EVs in real-world driving cycles [1]. Wang et al. (2021) presented a detailed review on isolated bidirectional dc–dc converter topologies and operation strategies for EV applications. The study categorized the converters as; PWM-based, dual active bridge and resonant type of which several other phase-shift control methods to improve performance have been discussed. The paper appeared to provide useful investigation for topology properties and control strategies, however its main concern is the performance of individual converter with no focus on dynamic topology selection or analytical comparison among systems under different EV operating conditions [2]. González-Castaño et al. (2022) where a composite EV power conversion system with flexible buck–boost DC–DC converter can have wide voltage regulation. The work focused on increasing motor efficiency by means of a flexible DC-link voltage control, and it was verified by thermal simulations,

segments.text: experimental results, and hardware-in-the-loop tests. Although being an efficient wide input voltage regulation was achieved in [3], the design assumed single topology selection and had no discussion on multi-selective topology according to operating modes. Tekin et al. (2023) presented a single-input multi-output buck–boost converter to obtain many voltage levels typical for EV application. The high voltage gain of the converter was adjustable by the duty cycle and a DSP-based PID controller was adopted for control. Despite the favorable voltage scaling potential of the topology, however, the control approach also remained static and was not tested for further dynamic transitions between several operating conditions such as regeneration and acceleration [4]. Zakaria et al. (2023) designed a hybrid interleaved nonisolated DC–DC converter with lower part count and high voltage gain for renewable energy and medium-voltage applications. The current ripple and voltage stress were also alleviated due to the interleaved implementation, while a PI-based controller was used for voltage regulation. Although the topology yielded high steady-state performance, it could only be used in fixed-use cases and did not meet the requirements of topology adaptability or EV specific duty control [5]. Nassary et al. (2024) analyzed a four-switch boost–buck AC/DC converter focusing on internal dynamic stability and power factor correction for EV charging. The authors introduced a damping RC circuit to solve the instability problem and verified their method by small-signal modeling and simulation. This work emphasized stability-oriented control, but it only concentrated on one converter topology and not comparative or topology-aware strategies [6]. Sangeetha & Ramachandran (2022) provided a wide technical review of EV subsystems such as electric machines, energy storage device and power electronic converter. They focused on propulsion, regenerative braking and energy management converter operation in various vehicles. The paper gave a comprehensive review on existing technologies, however the dynamic topology comparison and duty cycle adaption based framework was not proposed [7]. Islam et al. (2022) provided a comprehensive review of power converter topologies, control strategies and semiconductor devices for EVs. The research contrasted between the AC–DC, DC–DC and the DC–AC converters, while emphasizing advantages of wide-bandgap devices in order to achieve high efficiency and power density. Although the review was in depth, less attention had been paid to component-level optimization rather than system-level topology selection at dynamic EV operation scenarios [8]. Maroti et al. (2022) presented bidirectional DC−DC converter topologies and the role they play in grid-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-grid power flow transmission. The article focused on efficiency gains and improved reliability through next-level converter design. But that work considered fixed preset structures of the converter and couldn't handle dynamic transition between a number of topologies [9]. Hemavathi and Shinisha (2022) studied EV

The analysis shows to which degree dynamic operating conditions, selection of topology and topology-aware duty control are considered in other studies. This comparison demonstrates a lack of a coherent, system-wide methodology which makes evident the need for the presented topology-aware duty and selection process. 2.1 Literature Gap Summary Based on the reviewed literature, there have been remarkable DC–DC and bidirectional converter topologies as well as control methods and charging schemes for EVs. Previous works have investigated many high-efficiency converter topologies, soft-switching techniques and wide voltage-gain range operation mechanisms as well as advanced control strategies in scope of particular applications, like rapid charging, renewable generation integration and vehicle-to-grid scenario. However, in current literature the performance of the converter was tested for a preset operating point and topology, by considering a fixed conduction angle to maximise the transferred energy. Comparative analyses mostly have not taken into account dynamic transitions between modes of EV operation, but often concentrate on static performance criteria or topology level parameters. Moreover, advanced control methods tend to add higher computational complexity and practical deployment difficulties, thereby restraining their applicability in practice. Therefore, it can be inferred that there is no available common and practical framework for network topology dynamic selection jointly with application duty cycle separately in various topologies as well as fair performance comparison at the system level across realistic EV drives. This research gap motivates the design of the presented topology-aware duty and selection scheme. 3. System Model and Converter Topologies​ This section presents unique topology aware power conversion system for electric vehicle (EV) and the DC–DC converter topologies which are incorporated in proposed topology-aware duty and selection scheme. The goal is to provide a consistent system model to fairly compare different converter topologies for dynamic EV conditions.

Proposed TADS Algorithm​ 4.1 Motivation for Topology-Aware Selection Electric vehicle power converters work in very dynamic environments: the power and battery voltage [30][31], operating mode changes continuously during acceleration, cruising, regenerative braking and charging. Since no single DC–DC converter topology operates efficiently for the entire range, thermal performance is compromised due to topology suitability depending highly on both voltage conversion ratio and load level [32]. Losses of conduction and switching increase as a fixed topology is pushed to work at very high duty cycles, resulting in higher thermal stress and reliability problems [33]. Another reason is that the converter also deviates from its optimum working point to a large extent due to battery voltage changing with state of charge. These constraints inspire the topology-aware selection strategy selecting at run time the best converter configuration based on instantaneous power demand, voltage ratio and thermal restrictions and represent the basic elements of the proposed TADS (Topology-Aware Duty and Selection) algorithm. The architecture diagram of the proposed model is depicted in Figure 2.

Architecture of the proposed Topology-Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) framework for EV DC–DC power converters​ 4.2 TADS Algorithm Overview​ The Topology-Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) algorithm is a supervisory decision layer which dynamically selects correct DC—DC converter topology and its duty cycle for instantaneous operating conditions [34][35]. Power demand, battery to DC bus voltage ratio and thermal limit constraints are inputs to the algorithm reflecting electrical and thermal states of the EV power conversion system. TADS selects the most efficient topology that avoids high duty cycle operation based on predefined operating regions considering converter characteristics [36]. When the topology has been chosen, a topology- specific duty cycle is calculated based on the respective steady-state voltage conversion relation. The converter topology and the duty cycle command are thereby determined by the algorithm, so that efficient and thermally well balanced operation is achieved without needing advanced adaptive or optimization control strategies. It is worth pointing out that the proposed approach does not require any adaptive tuning, AI based or optimization controllers [40], but only requires duty cycle computation by algebraic expressions derived from converter basics, thereby resulting in no significant extra computational burdens and guaranteed control behavior. This method escapes the iterative calculation and real-time parameter identification, and it can be adapted to real-time EV application, meanwhile guarantees a good performance under dynamic behaviors [26]. 5. Simulation Setup and Performance Evaluation​ 5.1 Simulation Environment​ A MATLAB/Simulikk-based validation of the proposed topology-aware duty and selection framework is executed so as to model power electronics converters and EV operating situations with both accuracy and flexibility. All DC–DC converter topologies are described with switch models including non-ideal semiconductor components. The switching devices are described by datasheet base models of the devices (conduction resistance, switching energy loss, and parasitic elements) to model them in a realistic figure converter behavior. All topologies use a constant switching frequency in order to perform a fair comparison. Furthermore, a lumped 𝑓𝑠 electro-thermal model is coupled with the electric simulation, using thermal resistance parameters to relate the power loss to junction temperature rise. This coupled electrical–thermal modeling methodology provides a capability to assess efficiency and thermal stress under dynamic operating scenarios [16], [29]. 5.2 Drive Cycles Used In order to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm for practical EV driving situations, simulations based on standard driving cycles reflecting different driving environments are performed. This test captures various speed changes and dynamic power requirements typical of real world driving, as covered by the WLTC (Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Cycle). FTP-75 description expresses around-town driving that is most common in urban traffic. As an additional, a generic urban driving cycle is taken into account to discuss low-speed with repeated acceleration and regenerative braking. These drive cycles are converted to time-varying power demand profiles and imposed on the DC–DC conversion stage for effective system level assessment.

Based on the TADS approach, optimal topologies are used in each operating region, and 3.4% improvement of EUE compared to conventional converter configurations can be achieved. 6.1 Discussion​ The performance enhancements realized in the proposed TADS structure are largely achieved by being able to operate each DC–DC converter topology around its favorable voltage and power region instead of inefficient duty-cycle extremes that normally lead to high switching losses and thermal stress. With the strategy of dynamically choosing the most favourable topology according to instantaneous driving conditions, a more balanced loss distribution and better energy utilization across entire driving cycle is guaranteed. From a practical point of view, the obtained efficiency improvements, decreased switching losses and lower junction temperatures correspond directly to increased device lifetime, higher reliability and greater driving distance. The method is intrinsically scalable and the rule set of additional converter topologies or power levels can be simply extended without changing the main control architecture. Further this framework has industrial feasibility, there is no need for extra sensors or complex adaptive artificial intelligence–based controllers and real-time optimization, facilitating its integration within the existing EV power electronic structure using standard digital control platforms.

segments.text: 7. Conclusion​ In this paper, a novel Topology- Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) method is provided for electric vehicle DC–DC power conversion systems that significantly enhances the efficiency and thermal management in dynamic operating conditions. By dynamically choosing the optimal converter topology and calculating duty cycles specific to each topology based on closed-form solutions, the proposed method avoids compromises of dedicated-topology converters with complexity in control design. Simulation results carried out over standard EV drive cycles show that the proposed topology yields 2.8% higher system efficiency, an 18.6% lower peak switching loss and a reduced maximum junction temperature of 14.2%, compared to traditional converter configurations. Furthermore, the overall energy efficiency of utilization is enhanced by 3.4%, validating that the topology-aware approach can optimize system-level performance. Future work will be the experimental hardware validation of the presented concept under real driving conditions as well as an extension of the selection logic to take into account component aging and fault-tolerant operation. More research on multi-objective optimization regarding efficiency, thermal stress and reliability at the same time is also a next step to improve the robustness of power electronics in future generations EVs.
